utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are all the interpreters ready? Everybody hears me. Good morning, everybody. Does the Defence hear, does the Prosecution hear, General Blaskic, do you hear? We can now resume the hearing of Witness F. who is a Prosecution witness. Mr. Harmon? WITNESS F. (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Mr. President and your Honours, good morning counsel. Witness F., before we continue with where we left off in your testimony on Tuesday, let me clarify some points with you that you testified about on that day. On 16th April 1993, when you went to Niko Vidovic's house and you saw a nurse in the house with medical supplies, did it appear to you that a first aid station had been set up in the house before the attack on Ahmici had begun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. That is what it looked like to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Likewise, did it appear to you that a shelter had been set up in the basements of that particular house for the Croats before the attack on Ahmici began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We often stayed in that basement before the attack on Ahmici when the Serb airforce was shelling Busovaca and Vitez, and at the time, there were just wooden benches, but that morning, as I entered the basement there were beds there. On the beds there were pillows, covers, blankets, then there was a large wooden stove with a fire burning. There was a big pot on the cooking stove and one could smell beans cooking. The children were well clothed, they had their toys with them. There was a pram, everything seemed to be ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now Mr. President, if I could have, with the assistance of the usher, Exhibit 114A placed on the ELMO. Mr. President and your Honours and counsel, 114A is a different perspective of the previous exhibit and again a portion of what is Exhibit 53. There are numbers that are identical to the exhibit that appeared on 113A, that is numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 9, but on this particular exhibit, there are letters A through G which will be identified by the witness and as the court and counsel can see, instead of looking in the direction of Rovna, this, 114A, shows a perspective of the opposite direction, the direction depicting Ahmici and the village of Pirici. Witness F., during your testimony, you said that on 16th April, when you had left the basement, you saw the houses of Cazim Ahmic, Eso Ahmic and Sulejman Ahmic on fire. Can you, using the pointer, please point to the house of Cazim Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Cazim Ahmic's house (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You are indicating for the record the house on 114A with the circle and the letter D next to it. Can you point to the house of Eso Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You have placed the pointer on the circle marked with the letter C, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is Eso Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now can you point to the house of Sulejman Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You have placed your pointer on the circle with the letter B next to it on Prosecutor's Exhibit 114A, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was Sulejman Ahmic's house which I saw burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now you mentioned in your testimony, Witness F., that on 16th April in the morning a Bosnian Croat, identified you, came down and said two cousins by the name of Muharem and Nedzad Djidic had been killed. Can you point to their houses on Prosecutor's Exhibit 114A, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You have placed your pointer on the letter F. Whose house was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Djidic Nedzad's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you now indicate to the court where Muharem Djidic's house was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You have placed your pointer on the circle with the letter E next to it, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were in the basement of the house, you also heard that a man by the name of Fahrudin Ahmic had been killed. Can you indicate with your pointer where his house is located, indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 114A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, you have placed your pointer on the circle with the letter G next to it, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was Fahrudin Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Inside that circle, there are three structures. Was one of those houses the house of Fahrudin Ahmic and the other two structures, did they belong to his mother and father, Fatima Ahmic and her husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the house next to Fahrudin's was Fatima and Hasim Ahmic's and the third structure was a stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On that Prosecutor's Exhibit 114A there is a green line that is indicated. Do you see that line on Prosecutor's Exhibit 114A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What does that green line represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That green line marks the path along which we fled to Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I am finished with that exhibit for the time being, thank you. Witness F., on Tuesday, you also described a conversation that you had heard on the morning of 16th April while you were inside the house belonging to Niko Vidovic, and I have had a chance to review the transcript and show you a transcript of what is quoted, have I not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nodded).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, counsel, I am referring to page 3663, lines 12 through 14. After reviewing that quotation, did you inform me that that is not what -- it is not properly quoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please would you tell the court what you overheard being said by the men who were in the house of Niko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went outside (redacted) toilet, I saw, standing next to the house, Anto Kupreskic, Anto Dudzo and Frano Vidovic. Passing by them, Frano pointed with his hand to a small window, which led to the part of the basement where we were in and he said to the two of them, "look here, we should not kill them here, we should keep them and maybe some of our own will be captured and then we could exchange them". I realised then that we were captured, and that there was no question of any attack by the Mujahedin or anyone else. I saw the houses burning of Sulejman Ahmic and the others, and that was when I saw soldiers in the yard eating and talking about a job done. I went downstairs to the basement, I went up to (redacted) who was sitting on a wooden bench, I wanted to tell him what I had heard, and tears were coming down his face and he just nodded. Then I went to (redacted) and told him what I had heard. Then he started breathing heavily and he told me to pick up (redacted) and go outside so they could kill us outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, Witness F. Thank you very much for clarifying that point. Now let me return to where we left off in your testimony on Tuesday, and where we left off (redacted) (redacted), fled with Croats in the direction of (redacted), is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you cross a bridge over the Lasva river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we crossed the bridge called Radakov bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In Prosecutor's Exhibit 113A, is that bridge located -- if I could have the assistance of the usher, if we could place 113A on the ELMO. Mr. Usher, that is fine right there. Could you please, Witness F., with your pointer put the pointer on the bridge that (redacted) crossed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. After you crossed that bridge, could you tell the judges what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We crossed the bridge, and then groups of Croats, women and children, started going to various houses in Rovna. We stayed alone on the road, we were walking along that road, we reached a house in front of which a

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were walking (redacted) (redacted), there was a heavy artillery weapon firing bullets that were whizzing by our heads. I was afraid, (redacted), I tripped and fell, but (redacted), "do not be afraid, it is our people shelling Poculica". When I went in, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), "how come you are alive? How come you are here?". (redacted) tried to explain that we had spent two days and one night in Niko Vidovic's basement and that we had followed them. Then he got lost, first he whispered something with this (redacted), and then the (redacted) came in with a (redacted) and told us we could spend the night there, but we must leave before dawn and we must never tell anyone, if we survived, that we had spent the night there because (redacted) was afraid (redacted). We spent the night there and in the morning about 4.00, we went out, it was still dark and foggy --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you leave the house, Witness F., the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the (redacted) was afraid that somebody might come and find us there in that house, so we had to leave and we told (redacted) that we would head for UNPROFOR, across the fields, and (redacted) said, "I hope you succeed". That is how we left. We crossed the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again with the assistance of the usher, if we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 113A placed on the ELMO -- that is 114A. If the other one could be placed, 113A? Mr. Usher, the section I am interested in is the other half of that. If you could move it to the left? If you could continue moving it to the left so that numbers 5, 6 and 8 are visible on the ELMO. Mr. Usher, if you could move that to the right a little, I think 6 will become visible, and down a little. That is fine, thank you. Witness F., you (redacted) were attempting to get to the UNPROFOR base, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 113A with the number 7 on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I would like to interrupt for a second here. Is it absolutely necessary for the witness to have to indicate precisely? Perhaps there will be a challenge on the part of the Defence, but do you not think it is going perhaps a little too far? One can see how much this witness is suffering when she has to recall all these locations. If the witness says that she tried to reach the UNPROFOR base then she tried to reach the UNPROFOR base. It was already identified, a long time ago in fact. I do understand that it should be marked in the transcript that the witness has indicated 7 or 8 or the UNPROFOR base, but is it really necessary for your strategy, Mr. Harmon, to allow the witness to express herself the way she likes? If the Defence contests things then you can, of course, reply. This is really significant suffering this woman is experiencing in order to specify the houses, locations. The witness has just expressed what happened, because it was important for the Prosecution and for General Blaskic as well, but perhaps you could try to simplify somewhat, to clarify things, to get to the essential part of the matter. You are looking at someone who is suffering, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, I will proceed. Witness F., would you tell the judges then what happened after you crossed the bridge and what you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we crossed the bridge in the Lasva river valley, I saw four mortars and several soldiers taking off blankets from them or wiping them, I did not really watch. We tried to pass them without them noticing us and they did not, they probably thought we were Croats who had spent the time in Rovna, because there were many Croats spending the night in Rovna that day. So we followed the course of the Lasva river, the fog was rather thick and we wanted to get to UNPROFOR. For two days we had nothing to eat, we had not slept, we moved very slowly, and we approached the UNPROFOR base. We could already see the wire fence of the UNPROFOR in the distance. Then we heard a voice calling, "stop, stop". I saw three human figures approaching us from the field, they were running. (redacted) (redacted). One of the three knelt on the ground, one of the three soldiers who were approaching us knelt on the ground and targeted (redacted). At that moment, (redacted) called, "Ilija, stop, do not shoot". (redacted) "Ilija, stop", I called out (redacted), "stop, come back, come back", and he stopped and started running back. This soldier who was kneeling said, "who was it that said Ilija? I fuck his mother". They started towards us, they surrounded us, then I recognised Ilija Livancic, whom we had called Pican, and Jure Livancic, also Pican, and also a third soldier whom I had never seen before. Jure threw a shell across our heads, it went off, we fell to the ground, there was an explosion. Then he said, "get up you (redacted), you motherfuckers, where are you going to?" (redacted) (redacted) tried to tell him that we had spent the night at Jevdjo's with them, (redacted) (redacted). Jure told him, "shut up you motherfuckers, I will put a grenade into your mouth". Then he said, "let us take them back in case anybody from the UNPROFOR notices something", so they took us back about 100 metres and then Jure said, "stand closer to the river", and we did. (redacted) addressed Ilija once again and said, "Ilija please, do not kill women and children, let them go and do what you will with us". He said, "(redacted) and I am sorry, but we have been given orders to kill all the Muslims, and the Muslims will never live here again, and anyway I am not sorry (redacted) (redacted). It is all Alija Izetbegovic's fault, the motherfucker". Then I took (redacted) (redacted), we lined up and they said, "get closer", and Jure said, "you see this Lasva river? She took many Muslims away and she will take you too". (redacted) (redacted), his wife and three children, we were all crying, no one was saying anything. (redacted), (redacted) who had put my

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) She caught hold of my hand, I put my other hand on my stomach, (redacted), and then the soldier said to Jure, "how am I going to do it? Am I going to kneel down or do it standing", and he said, "you will have to kneel down because they are too small, you will not be able to get them all". Then I closed my eyes and I could not see anything, I was waiting for the bullet. I could hear the guns being cocked and I was waiting. I heard an unusual sound, and I saw a bird flying over our heads. I begged the bird to tell (redacted) where we were, and at that moment, Ilija, who was about 20 metres away from me, said, "wait, wait, somebody is waving from Nenad's house", and Jure said, "we will not stop, we have a job to do, Ilija. We must do it". Ilija cried out, "Jure, do as you have been told, run up there and see what they want". Jure did not want to and then he repeated the order, he came back soon and he said somebody was waving from Nenad's house. He told us to pick up (redacted) and follow him. Jure went in front and this unknown soldier and Ilija behind us. Jure was threatening as to what Nenad would do with us as we went along. Ilija was saying how all the Muslims had been killed and he said (redacted), Rasim, he was our schoolfriend, he too was killed in front of his house". We got close to Ilija Pican's house, Livancic's, and his father was standing in front, who came up and said, "where did you catch them? They tried to get to UNPROFOR. I would kill all of them, all (redacted), I would take them away". Then Ilija said, "you old man, you are not the one to decide. Nenad will decide". Nenad Santic was standing in front of his house with Drago Josipovic and they were talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F., let me interrupt you there for just a minute. These three soldiers who informed you that they had orders to kill all the Muslims, can you tell the court first of all how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore camouflage military uniforms, and they had the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All three of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you arrived at Nenad Santic's house, was he there with Drago Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he stood in front of the door of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How was Drago Josipovic dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wore camouflage military uniform and had a white belt, like military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How did Nenad Santic appear dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nenad Santic wore a camouflage uniform, he had a cap on his head. He looked at us, (redacted), he told him -- he said, "where did you think you were going?". He said, "we were going towards the UNPROFOR. We did not know ourselves where to go". He started laughing, "you think that UNPROFOR would help you?".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F., let me just clarify one thing. You said Nenad Santic was in a camouflage uniform. Did he have any white belts that signified that he may have been a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a wide white belt on his jacket and the other one had -- Drago had the thin white belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia that indicated they were in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day I did not see it, but I knew that they were members of the HVO, because all Croats that I knew were swearing to Nenad Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, Witness F. Would you please continue then with what occurred in front of Nenad Santic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ilija said, "Nenad, what shall I do with them? Why did you call us?". He told him, "I thought that it was somebody more important", and Jure said at that point, "Nenad, you know that nobody ran away of us, so they will not either". Ilija said again "Nenad, what shall I do with them?". Nenad said, "I do not know what to do. Do whatever you want, fuck their mothers, they are not interesting. You can also take them where the other garbage is, in Ilija's shop". Ilija said, "so tell me what to do". He said, "take them to the shop". Ilija's brother Mirko showed up from somewhere, he was going in front of us and he said "cross the road slowly to go to Ilija's shop", that is where all the survivors were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You arrived at a location that was a shop and was also a house, was it not? It had two purposes, a house and a shop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the property of Miso Livancic, called Pican. Before the attack to Ahmici it was a shop and we were calling it the shop at Ljiljo's. That is how we called the man who kept the shop. In front of that shop, Anto Babic was standing. He opened the door for us, we entered. I was the last one to come into the shop and in there there were women and children. Nobody was saying a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know how many women and children were in that shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were 85, because later we were counted. At the time when I entered, I thought that we were 1,000. Women were crying, children were crying, they were Muslim children and women, that I knew. Ahmic Fatima, she was sitting up front, she got up, (redacted) and told him, "my dear son, are you alive? Yesterday they killed my Fahran, today my Hasim was taken, Amir, Munib Heleg. My son, they will kill you too, women, let us get up to protect the three of them". Some women got up, the three of them sat down. I turned around, and behind the door, I saw a man who was all muddied, who was all singed, and I asked Fatima who that was, she said it was Jula Brandza, she said, "I did not know he was alive". (redacted) (redacted). Then we again kissed each other goodbye and we only waited when somebody was going to open the door. The time was passing and the door opened and at the door Nikoslav Plavcic was at the door, called Slikica, and he said, "women, I did whatever I could for you. You will be taken to the railroad station, you will be exchanged".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F., were there any Croats in detention in that shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no Croats, there was only Anto Papic, called Babic, who was guarding us in front of the door. He was wearing military camouflage uniform and carried a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you taken then from that location where you were detained to another location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went outside and Nikica Slikica told us to go two and two and not to make any noise, not to try to escape, that we would be exchanged, that we would be taken to the free territory and he mentioned Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he have any form of mobile communication with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was walking in ahead of us, he had a small bag over his shoulder and at the belt, he had a walkie-talkie. He was talking something in it, but I did not hear what it was. We went down the road and while we were walking, vehicles were passing us and there were soldiers in camouflage uniforms there and we were afraid all the time that some of them would stop and catch up with us. We went to the railroad station, Nikica said to go towards the school. In the school yard, when we got there, there were soldiers in both black and camouflage uniforms. They were waiting for us there, (redacted) (redacted). As we entered the school building, they separated us. The last I saw was a soldier in a black uniform who was putting the barrel of his gun (redacted) (redacted) in the opposite direction. Then I entered the class room with my children and suddenly the door opened and a soldier came in and he said, "get up, get up", and I got up and he put the barrel of his gun here (indicates) and he said, "why are you crying? Why are you whining? Fuck your (redacted) mother". I said, "I am afraid, I do not know where (redacted) are" and (redacted) were crying too. He said, "shut up, I cannot stand it when (redacted) are crying". I put my hands on both of their mouths and he said again, "why are you crying?", and I said, "I did not know where my (redacted)". He said, "you think we are killing someone? We do not kill anyone. You Muslims, you are trash. If I hear you cry again, I will kill you, fuck your (redacted) mother".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F., to your left there are some tissues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness F., would you like us to take a break for a few moments? Would you like us to suspend the hearing for about ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nodded).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You prefer to take a break? Very well, we will resume in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing, please proceed. Witness F., do you feel better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you have any other problems, please do not hesitate to say it and, of course, the Tribunal will do everything it can so that your testimony can be conducted under conditions that are not too difficult for you. I am sure that the Prosecutor will be sensitive to that. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F., did you remain at the Dubravica school until 5th May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Between the time you arrived at the Dubravica school and 5th May, did you ever (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him when they were going out, when a soldier was escorting them to a truck and their hands were like (indicates), and later (redacted) told me that every day, every night they were coming for them, that they were digging trenches for them at Krcevine, at Kratine, Mahala and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F., you indicated that (redacted) were like "this". Could you show the court what you mean by "this"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several men who were walking and they had their hands like this and they were going to the truck. Behind them there was a soldier with a rifle escorting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, your Honour, the witness indicated with both of her hands behind her head that that was the position of the (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you like, Mr. Harmon, but I would like to emphasise that the Tribunal did understand what was meant when you said that a prisoner has his hands behind his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F., was (redacted) when he was digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was wounded in (redacted). He was digging trenches at Krcevine and on that occasion, two of these prisoners died from the school in Dubravica and several of them were wounded and he was one of those who were wounded. One of the more seriously injured persons there needed to have an IV held for him on the way to Travnik, and one of the soldiers whom (redacted) knew who lived in (redacted) and he asked (redacted) whether he would be able to hold the IV bag while this person was being transferred to Travnik, and while (redacted) stayed in (redacted), I did not know of his fate. Another day, a Croat soldier came and brought his jacket and threw that jacket into the class room there. I did not dare approach it until he left the room and then when he did, I approached and took the jacket and recognised it (redacted). I overheard the soldiers in the hallway saying that some Muslims were killed and some were injured and I did not know what happened to my (redacted) until I reached Zenica. When I came to Zenica, I was accommodated in an orphanage and the director of this orphanage went on the air to ask whether anybody knew anything (redacted), and several days later, she said that (redacted) while my (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have concluded my examination of Witness F. and I would now ask that Prosecutor's Exhibit 113A be admitted into evidence and 113B, which is the legend, be admitted into evidence as well, but the legend 113B be placed under seal and remain confidential. I would also move to introduce Prosecutor's Exhibit 114A and the legend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There are no comments from the Defence, therefore we will put the exhibit under seal. This is for identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am moving into evidence, not for identification purposes but for purposes for the Chamber to consider all of the exhibits, but I only ask that 113B, the legend, be placed under seal, because identifying information is contained in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I thought I had understood. Anyway, now I turn to the Defence. Witness F., we are here before a Tribunal in which when there is somebody who is accused of serious crimes who is in the box of the accused, you understand we must give the floor to the Defence as well to ensure an equitable system. You will now be asked questions by one of Colonel Blaskic's attorneys. He will ask questions. The Tribunal, of course, is here to ensure that the questions asked continue to protect you as best as possible, and this Tribunal will hear all of your statements in order to reach truth. Turning to the Defence now, who is going to do the cross-examination. Is it Mr. Hayman, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am going to conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only have one or two questions which might identify the witness, so I would suggest that we turn off the sound in the gallery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now move into a private session. Registrar, would you please ensure that that is done, and as soon as we are ready, Mr. Nobilo can begin his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, the witness is still being protected, do not be concerned, these are simply specific measures that had to be carried out. Mr. Nobilo, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Witness F., you stated that you saw the Jokers and the Vitezovi soldiers. How do you distinguish between them? How do you distinguish the unit of Vitezovi, their members and Jokers and their members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they have different names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe these name tags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I draw it for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, can you describe it in words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vitezovi wore black uniforms and they had the name written, "Vitezovi", and Jokers had the insignia there (indicates) and also had the name "Jokers" on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about these units? How do you separate them out from the rest of them and what kind of information do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am no military expert, (redacted) (redacted), so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, the person who came down to the (redacted) with you for a (redacted) and he was ordered to kill you, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody came down to the (redacted) with me, (redacted), came and he said that he was ordered to take the three of them so that they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what his real name is? (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the Plavcic stables, how far was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), so I do not know how far that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tell me, how many women and children were going with you across the Lasva river to (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the entire Croatian population there, women and children. They were moving in groups and we did not go with them, we were the last ones who crossed the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the entire civilian population was moved out that way. Were there any men with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but Nenad met them and he said, "you motherfuckers, why are you leaving the frontline positions? Come with me". He said that to Jevdjo Vidovic who was walking in front of us. He said to Jevdjo, "you gypsy motherfucker, do not leave your position".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the atmosphere like, was there panic there or was it disciplined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not much panic, people were going to take shelter, because they saw that the Plavcic stables were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did anyone say that the Muslims were attacking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Jevdjo said on 16th April at 5.10 in the morning that 8,000 Mujahedins were coming and were attacking Vitez and that we should take shelter and Mujahedins do not make any difference between Muslim and Croat population and we trusted him, so we went with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But when you were going towards Rovna, when you were leaving Zume, before you left, did anybody bring any word of some kind of danger, why were people fleeing at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I only know that (redacted), opened the door and she said that the Plavcic's stables were on fire and that the best thing would be for everyone to take shelter in Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Plavcic is a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was in Mahala, it was not in Zume, about a kilometre maybe from Zume, in the direction of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So a kilometre from Zume from where you lived, the Croat stables went up in flames?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But you heard it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any mention of soldiers from Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I only know that Ivica Jevdjo at one point came to the basement and said that the Jokers and the Vitezovi found out about us and he has to protect himself because now it is his life that is to be risk. He turned to the women and said, "women, go find your men and remember our agreement to protect them". When I came to the school, I learned about the soldiers from Herzegovina. There was talk about them, there were soldiers caught there and I saw an ID card from somebody who was from the (redacted), and (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recall when you talked to the investigators beforehand and you stayed at -- some soldiers from Herzegovina found out about you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) had camouflage, a pair of trousers and a soldier's jacket and (redacted) had a camouflage uniform and he had a jacket which he later took off because he must have been hot because he was running after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There was a third unknown soldier. Did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was talking to (redacted), not to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the grenade that they threw, how far from you did it fall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned Nenad Santic and that all the Croats that you know sweared on him. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was before the attack on Ahmici. I was a neighbour and I had friends from school and the neighbours with whom I talked and they were talking about Nenad, how, "while we have Nenad, we should not be afraid of anything". They were proud of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well Nenad, (redacted). Where did he live exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was with Picans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his position in the local commune, that is in military terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you, I do not know anything about the military, I was not interested in that. I only knew that from their conversations among the Croats that Nenad was the commander, but who he was commanding, that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he commanding these neighbours of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned Anto Papic, Babic, who guarded you. Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Papici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where is this in relationship to (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is across the road but in the opposite direction. You take a different road towards (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is the difference, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) .

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So again your (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you came to that shop, was there any shooting going on in that area or was there a lull?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a lull when we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So there was no shooting around the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Nikica Slikica Plavcic, (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was part of the local commune of Santici. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted). In the school where you ended up, which unit was controlling it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, the HVO members were coming into the class rooms and I saw at one point a man with whom I went to school, Bralo. He was looking at us, how miserable we were, he had the HVO insignia. Some wore black uniforms, some wore camouflage uniforms. At first I did not dare look at them because the first time I did, one of the soldiers told me that we should always close our eyes when they come in, because we were not worthy of looking at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you came to that school, you said mostly there were people in black uniforms. Were there any insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said before, I did not look because I was ordered not to look around much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is all, your Honour. I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The cross-examination is complete, I now turn to my colleagues to see whether they have any additional questions they would like to ask. But before that, I do see Mr. Harmon who perhaps would like to make some clarification. So first we will have the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I had almost felt that. Now I turn to my colleagues, Judge Riad, who is going to ask several additional questions, after which we will be complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will call you Witness F. I am sorry if I do not treat you properly and say your name. I just would like to know, when you were arrested by this man called Ilija and some other persons with him, he told you that they had been given orders, this is what you said, they have been given orders to kill the Muslims and that the Muslims will never live there any more, that the Lasva river is full of Muslim corpses. When he spoke of having been given orders, did he indicate from where these orders came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not say where the orders came from, but he just said, "we have been given orders to kill all the Muslims and the Muslims will never live here again".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he appear to be a regular soldier, according, of course, to your limited knowledge, the way he was dressed, the way they were talking, the way they were perhaps receiving messages from other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He appeared to me to be an ordinary soldier, and I think he was giving orders to Jure Pican, because at one point he said to Jure, "do as I have told you, do as you have been ordered to do".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So there was some kind of hierarchy, as if it was in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Jure is older than Ilija, but Jure was listening to what Ilija told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mention that (redacted) when he was digging trenches. What happened to him after that? You did not tell us this, the rest of his experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took them out to dig trenches daily, and then to one place one day and to another place another day. One day he was digging trenches at Krcevine in the direction of Bukva, and there was shooting all around, and the soldiers that were guarding them were under shelter, whereas they had to continue digging. Suddenly, that is what he told me when he came to Zenica, he felt that his arm had dropped into the trench. He caught hold of it and he saw behind him a man who was covered in blood and holding on to his leg. Then he called the guard, he knew him by name and he said -- he told him that they had been wounded and he called back that they should crawl back to the house and that is what they did. Then he bandaged (redacted) and he tied the leg of the other person with his belt, and then he asked (redacted) whether he was capable of holding the intravenous infusion as he would be driven to Travnik for the benefit of this other man who was wounded in the leg. He said that he could, and I think that the fact that he said that he could saved him, because otherwise the Croats would have certainly taken him back to the camp, and that is how he got to Travnik. At that time, there were Croats and Muslims together in Travnik, they were still together, and members of both armies went there for treatment, to a joint hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were these trenches exactly which they were digging? Did your (redacted) inform you about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that day that when he was wounded, the trenches were at Krcevine, in the direction of Bukva, between Bukva and Krcevine. Krcevine was a Croatian village and Bukva was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There was fighting going there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How did he get wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. He just said that he felt his arm twitch and fall into the trench, as he was trying to use a shovel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that other people died, two others died, so there must have been shooting then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You do not know where from it came. Were they shot by the Croats, by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. He himself does not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But he knows that there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just for my knowledge, what (redacted)? Were they harmed or are they safe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not harmed. I stayed in the elementary school in Dubravica and then UNPROFOR took me to Zenica and (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHBUDDEEN
utterances.text: Witness F., did you see any Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw any in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In some places in your evidence, you spoke of seeing Vitezovi and Jokers and HVO soldiers. I want to ask you a question about the Vitezovi soldiers. Did you see the insignia which they wore, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were the insignia? Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vitezovi had the word "Vitezovi" and the Jokers the word "Jokers". As far as I know, and saw, the Jokers wore camouflage uniforms that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. Did you at any stage see soldiers from all three groups together or in the vicinity of each other? Did you see Jokers together with Vitezovi and with HVO people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only once or twice in the school in the class room, when they came in, men, Croats, whom I knew would come in who were HVO members, and they came in together with the Jokers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see, thank you. One last point. You said to us that you spent a night in the home of a (redacted), is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And (redacted) called you in and offered you shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) was looking for the (redacted) (redacted). (redacted) was not looking for any Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. I am glad you clarified that. But (redacted) nevertheless gave you shelter that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had already entered, and (redacted) did not know us, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in that house, a man was sitting there, a neighbour of ours who recognised us and then (redacted) realised that we were Muslims and (redacted) was terrified, her hands started shaking and (redacted) was saying, "why on earth did you have to come here?".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHBUDDEEN
utterances.text: I am grateful to you for that explanation which should have been clear enough to me from your earlier evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness F., I wanted to ask you whether at any point during these tragic events you heard anybody say anything or hear about Colonel Blaskic, around you, in the cellar, at the school or anywhere else, did people speak about Blaskic, or not at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the 16th, 17th and 18th April, I never heard anyone mention Blaskic, but before 16th April, I did hear his name mentioned on television and on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you make the connection between the responsibilities that he had and the events, or did other people make any kind of connection between him and what was going on around you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At this time that the events took place, which went over several days. Did you or any of the people near you make any connection between what they had seen on television in the previous weeks when the accused would appear on television in his uniform and the time when these dreadful events took place? Was this connection made or not? Just answer very simply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, throughout that time, we believed that the Croats would not hurt us and we believed their stories, that they were holding us only on account of the Serbs and that they would not hurt the Muslims. Then we saw that they had betrayed us, all those on television as well as our neighbours. They were all working against us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Turning again to my colleagues, who have no additional questions, the Tribunal is very sensitive to your having come here to confront this difficult work of testimony and cross-examination. Things are now complete. You are being taken care of by the Witness and Victim Unit, who will ensure that you continue to be protected. Perhaps we should draw the curtains before the witness leaves. Might that not be better? The Registrar has just told me that we will take a break, because the testimony of Witness F. is complete. We will resume in 20 minutes, that is at 12.00. For the time being, please do not move and we will take care of you to be sure that you are properly protected. The hearing is now suspended and will resume at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor? It is Mr. Cayley, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours. We are ready to proceed with the next witness, who is Mr. Abdulah Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did not have my microphone adjusted properly, at least the console was not right. Would you repeat yourself, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours. The Prosecutor is ready to proceed with the next witness, who is Mr. Abdulah Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is not a protected witness then, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like just to speak with the Registrar for a moment. (Pause). All right, can we have the following witness brought in, please? About how much time have you scheduled for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would estimate, your Honour, between two and three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the witness stand first. The usher should know what to do. Please have the witness stand. First, you are Mr. Abdulah Ahmic, is that correct? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you Abdulah Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Abdulah Ahmic, we are going to give you a declaration which you will be asked to read before giving testimony. It must be read out loud, sir. ABDULAH AHMIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may be seated. Mr. Abdulah Ahmic, the Office of the Prosecutor in the trial which is being conducted against Tihomir Blaskic before the International Tribunal has called you. I believe the Office of the Prosecutor has explained how things will be conducted. You are before judges who will listen to you. You may speak without hatred, without fear and now I will turn to the Prosecutor, who will begin to ask you questions. Once he has finished asking his own questions, you will then be asked to answer questions asked by the counsel for Colonel Blaskic. In the name of the International Criminal Tribunal, it is Mr. Cayley who is going to conduct the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, one point before we begin. During the war, Mr. Ahmic was very seriously injured and he has lost partial hearing in one ear so I would only ask for the court to be aware that he may, at times, have a problem in hearing me. If he does, he will let me know. That is a point for the court and for the party opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, we will take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you can leave the microphone on in front of you. Mr. Ahmic, you are of Bosnian nationality, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you are of the Muslim religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Ahmici, municipality of Vitez, on 29th January 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How old are you, Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Before the war years, had you travelled widely throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Serbia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, can you describe to the judges how life was in Ahmici and the Lasva Valley before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We lived, one might say, in harmony, without any problems. Our life was quite normal, the way all other normal people live.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you broadly describe to the court the different ethnic groups that lived in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were the Bosniaks, the Croats and the Serbs. The Bosniaks and the Croats were in the majority, the Serbs were a small group, and in terms of religion, the Bosniaks were Muslims, the Croats were Catholic and the Serbs were Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The village of Ahmici, your home, what was the composition, the ethnic composition of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Ahmici, Bosniaks lived and the Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Prior to the war, do you remember any problems between the Catholics and the Muslims in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just very briefly explain to the court when the trouble began in the village of Ahmici between the two different groups, the Catholics and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the problems in our municipality as a whole started after the multi-party elections. This was probably reflected upon the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I know you were unemployed shortly before the war, but where did you work before you were unemployed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I worked in a military factory in Vitez for a year and a half to two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you are familiar with the military industrial complex factories in the Lasva valley in the Vitez and Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I worked in all three or actually this was one factory, but it had three different sections, and I worked in all three.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By April 1992, who was in charge of these factories, who was running them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The factories were jointly run, they were run both by Muslims and Croats, and some Serbs were among the executives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By April 1993, were the Bosniaks still working in these factories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very few of them were still working, they were mostly laid off or "put on hold", as we called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were these people excluded from the work place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In April 1993, who was running these factories, who was in charge of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April 1993, full control over the factories was held by the Croats. They even brought some soldiers from Herzegovina, allegedly to guard the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a military formation of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I know you are not an expert on the HVO, but can you briefly describe to the court your impression of the HVO in the municipality of Vitez and in your village, Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. The HVO was not just a military formation, it was actually the authority. The HVO was in power and they were involved in all walks of life. They were more than just a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "all walks of life", what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They influenced the economy, the political life, the cultural life, and virtually -- how can I put it -- it was a kind of military rule that interfered in all aspects of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992, and up until April 1993, were there organised units of the Bosnian army garrisoned in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could not really talk of an army. We had the Territorial Defence, which was in the process of being formed, but it was more of a civil protection factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So there was no Bosnian army in Ahmici during the time period that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. One cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in Ahmici, were you a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were its functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The functions of Territorial Defence were exclusively to hold guard duty during the night, and to protect property, in case of any unforeseen incidents, like torching and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did all members of the Territorial Defence have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many would you estimate were armed with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my estimate, only a third of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the Croats in your village join the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did they join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had the HVO, they joined the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Ahmic, before the war, with whom did you live in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived with my father, mother, three sisters and a brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your father's name was Alija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in 1993, he was aged 57?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And your mother's name was Latifa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in 1993, she was aged 49?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your brother was Muris?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he was aged 27 in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then your sisters, Smaila was aged 24, Sabira 23 and Alma aged 16, and that was their ages in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us briefly talk about the events in Ahmici in October 1992. Am I right in saying that the villagers erected a barrier across the Busovaca Vitez road on 19th October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did they do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croats, or rather a report came that the Croats were being mobilised in Busovaca, Kiseljak, Kresevo Kakanj, because there had been a conflict broken out in Novi Travnik, and they had mobilised very strong forces which they wanted to transfer to Novi Travnik. So we set up this barrier to prevent them in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there a factory that the Croats were interested in in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a struggle for a military factory, most probably that was why the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the HVO tell you to remove the barrier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What happened on the early morning of 20th October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 6.30, they started shooting at our men at the roadblock. Our people ran for shelter and about 7.00 they hit with a recoiless gun the minaret of the mosque, and about 8.00 an infantry attack started against our houses. The houses were hit by incendiary shells, as well as our stables.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you removed the barrier, or not you personally but members of the village removed the barrier that morning, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the roadblock no longer existed already. At about 6.30 the barrier no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the women and children who live near to the road were evacuated to the upper part of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were involved in that process, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many civilians were evacuated from the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can talk in percentages, I would say about 80 per cent of the people were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of the Muslim population of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were they mostly women and children or men as well as women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly women and children, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any damage to property during this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they set fire to four houses and about ten stables and other smaller structures, and they damaged some houses too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you recall the names of the owners of the property that was destroyed and the particular piece of property that that person had destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The houses of Mehmed Ahmic, Hahrudin Pjanic, two houses of his were set on fire, Sakib Pezer's house and I think Sefik Pezer's house too. Those were the houses. As for the stables, Alija Ahmic's, my father's stable was the first to be set on fire. Then Suljeman Ahmic's stable, Hidjaret Bilic's, Sakib Pezer's, Sefik Pezer's, Kasim Ahmic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What happened to the -- excuse me, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Hahrudin Pjanic's stable was also burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. What happened to the livestock that was in your father's stable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother Muris let them free and they were roaming around simply and under the shower of bullets, he somehow managed to let them go, so they were not hit, they were not killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was anybody killed during this attack on the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Halid Pezer, who was a minor, he was hit by a sniper. The sniper was operating from Ivo Papic's house. A bullet whizzed right by my head too. That was the bullet that hit Halid Pezer right in the heart. Dragan Papic carried the sniper often, he was the son of Ivo Papic. This was before this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How old was Halid Pezer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was 15 or 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When did the attack by the HVO on the village stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just before nightfall, on 19th October.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did negotiations take place with the local HVO after this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were negotiations and our people, actually they wanted us to surrender all our weapons, the settlement of Zume surrendered their weapons. They were mixed, of mixed ethnic origin. They all had to surrender their weapons, they wanted the upper part of the village to surrender too, but our people did not agree. They did give up four rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "they" demanded that you give up your weapons, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The four weapons that you refer to that were given up, to whom did those weapons belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those rifles had been taken from military policemen who were disarmed at the roadblock on 19th October.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They were HVO military policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did HVO soldiers stay by the houses, in the houses by the roadside after the attack was completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they stayed there and I think they stayed for about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The civilians who had fled the village, when did they return to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They returned gradually, and this went on for about a month. My family was the last to return a month later to their own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the atmosphere in the village between the period of October 1992 and 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was rather tense. We were in a kind of occupation zone, one might call it. There were frequent incidents, shootings, explosions and threats by certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was responsible for these shootings, explosions and threats in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was being done by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you give any specific examples of this type of behaviour that went on in the village in this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. In the settlement called Zume on the main road, they blew up a car. A large amount of explosive was used for this. Then I can mention another example, it was Ramadan and we were praying on the grass and when the people were going home, returning from prayer, near Mirko Vidovic's house, a very strong explosion was -- occurred very close to these people, so this was a way of intimidating the people. There were also provocations using infantry weapons constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: During this time in the evenings, were you able to freely travel around the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. They would not let us carry any kind of weapons, they introduced a curfew, movement was limited until 9 or 10, and they were the masters of the communication line between Vitez and Busovaca, so that there was very little movement during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say that, "they were the masters of the communication line," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to the HVO, because they had the checkpoints in many locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you refer to the "communication line", are you referring to the road between Busovaca and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From your own personal observations, was there any change in the HVO between October 1992 and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were great changes. They were arming themselves intensively. They were bringing in extra personnel, probably from Herzegovina, and there was a lot of material that was being brought in, we were noticing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. We will now move forward in time to 16th April 1993, but first of all, I would like to place in front of you Exhibit 115. If you recall, when you and I were speaking before your testimony, you made some marks on an aerial photograph, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I arranged for those marks to be transferred into this form by way of a computer-generated image.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you checked these marks on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you happy with the various positions and the circles that are drawn on the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you tell the court what you remember of what happened on the morning of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 5.30, we were awakened by the artillery fire. Donje Selo was attacked, this was near the road, and then the middle village also, Grabovi, they were under attack. We were at home, my father, mother, three sisters and my brother was sleeping down in the basement. The first thing I noticed was that a house was on fire. It belonged to Sukrija Ahmic. After that, I was watching from the window -- in fact before that, I called my brother Muris and we consulted on what to do. He said, "we cannot go anywhere, because the house has been surrounded by soldiers". Then I looked out of the window, I saw soldiers in two locations. Just a moment, please. In the location marked number 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you wait, because there is no image on the screen as yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can it be seen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Not yet. If we just wait one moment. (Pause). Mr. President, I think everybody has a copy of this photograph in front of them, so if the technical wizardry is failing us, we can still continue. Mr. Ahmic, could you first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think yes, that would be simpler. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you first of all inform the court of the location of your house, your family house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house is at the location marked with 1. Continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I observed from the window of my house and I observed five to six soldiers near Fahrudin Ahmic's house, that is the location marked with number 2, and the location number 3, that is Hajra Ahmic's house, also four to five soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what the soldiers around Ahmic Fahrudin's house were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers at the Fahrudin's house, I saw that one was carrying a gas canister and was setting it on fire and the others were just there around the house. That means they were all setting it on fire. The other house they did not set on fire, they were just walking around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say the soldier was carrying a gas can. By that, do you mean a gasoline can?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see them pouring fuel on to Fahrudin's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the soldiers that were around Fahrudin's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised one from Nadioci, he is a man in his middle age. I used to see him a lot by the beach down in Nadioci, and he used to play an accordion quite often. I never learned his name, but I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to look into the centre of Ahmici at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The central part of the village, as I said, Sukrija Ahmic's house and probably Sakib Ahmic's houses up in Grabovi were already on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you observe any traffic on the main road at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I observed a convoy, they were going down towards Busovaca, that was the convoy of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the court what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my having observed all this, I heard the voice of a man who was shouting, "hurry up, do not stay by this house", meaning Fahrudin's house, "move over here to this house", meaning our house. After that I heard a detonation of a grenade and then two shots fired from small weapons, infantry weapons. Three to four minutes later, no more than that, the entrance door to our house was just showered with bullets. We were in the kitchen, so nobody was hurt, but the door was riddled with bullets. Then they started hitting the door so that they would break it down, and my father and I came out and we said, "do not, we will open up the door", so we opened up the door and we saw two soldiers. They were painted -- they had their faces painted like in camouflage. They had bullet-proof vests and they had automatic rifles with collapsible butts. The first thing they asked of us was they asked for weapons. Then I am going to now describe you how they looked, these two soldiers. One was about 1.9 metres tall, big, blond, he had like a punk haircut and the other one was about 1.70 tall, he had long wavy hair down to his shoulders and he was much more thin. The big one was pretty rude, and the smaller one was more quiet. The tall one ordered me to come out of the house to the yard, and he ordered the younger soldier to guard us and my mother and sisters remained in the hallway and were just watching everything silently, then he entered the house to search it. After having searched it, he returned. At that time, I saw the UN convoy passing down the road in the direction of Busovaca, and when this man came out of the house, he ordered the younger one, he said, "follow the orders", and the younger one says, "I will not". He repeated this two more times, and then to both these orders, he answered, "I cannot do it". Then the big one says, "okay, I am going to carry out the order, but you will remember this", and he said it in a threatening voice. Then he ordered me and my father to pass around the southern side of the side, and he ordered that the younger one to guard my mother and sisters.
