When we came around the house, we saw our brother Muris, he was lying on the ground on his stomach and he was dead, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, can I interrupt you at this point? If the witness could be shown Exhibit 116/1. Mr. Usher, if you could actually take the photograph out of the plastic file, and place the first photograph on to the ELMO. Mr. Ahmic, who is this a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my brother Muris, who was killed, as I was just relating.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How old was he at the time that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think this is the only photograph you have of your brother, but this was taken a number of years before 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this photograph was taken when he completed his secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please continue. Mr. Usher, if you could replace the previous exhibit on to the ELMO, because we have not finished with that yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came to the spot where my brother was lying dead, the tall soldier ordered my father to step out two steps. My father was barely able to do that, and then from one metre distance, he fired a bullet directly in his temple, he was I think dead right on the spot, and then he told me to step out -- to make two steps forward. Then from the left side he fired a bullet and the bullet came in here and came out here (indicates), and then he turned around and went back to the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, if I can interrupt you, because this is important, can you please indicate to the judges where the bullet entered your head and where it left your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, I do not know if you can see it, but here, this is where the bullet entered and this is where it exited, so there is a scar here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the bullet entered at your right temple and it exited at your right cheek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the left temple and it came out -- exited at the right cheek.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And passed through your soft palette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, through my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which is how you survived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, probably he was not aiming right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To he turned around and for a moment I was still standing and I saw that I was still alive. Then I faked a fall, as if I was dead. He turned around, he was not sure about something, but when he saw my falling, he turned back and went to the yard from where he had brought us. For several moments, I remained lying there, and after about a minute or two, I lifted my head, looked around, if there were any soldiers I could not see anyone. Then there is on the west side of my house a slope, so I ran down towards the main road. This is marked with number 7, so that is the line, and I came to the location marked with number 4. I came to the road and at that point, there were no vehicles on the road. I sat there for about three or four minutes. At that moment, I saw soldiers coming from the direction of -- it is marked with number 5, and then you see those three arrows. There was nothing else I could do, there was like a small bridge, there was a creek there, and I went into this canal, so in other words I climbed down into it from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, can I interrupt you at this point? You said that you went into a small canal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the photograph the position of this small canal or I think probably it is better called a pipe under the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates). It is the location marked with number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe this space that you occupied to the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I climbed down from up above in this direction (indicates), and I was observing the soldiers who were running and spreading out into formation. Before I climbed down, I already saw some houses on fire. That is when I first observed soldiers, the houses were already burning and from this position, I observed a group of about 30 to 40 soldiers, so that would be a platoon size, and they were spreading into formation. Ivica Safradin, called Cico, was there, I recognised him, I used to work with him in the Vitezit company in Vitez. He was leading a group of military police, there were five or six soldiers who wore the military police insignia. In this group, there were some men who were even in civilian clothes with weapons and in this group of soldiers who arrived and who were taking positions, I also recognised Dragan Santic from the village of Rovna, he used to be an auto mechanic, and Nikica -- Ivica Santic, I think that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniform of the military policemen that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had belts, they had white insignia on their arms. I recognised them only insignia I recognised with one soldier, it was the special units, so I recognised even that insignia, and I also recognised -- I do not know, Ivica or Nikica Santic, he was from Mahala, he was married with a woman from Nadioci, he had a big moustache and he worked in Zenica, but he was from Santici. I also recognised Blaz Totic from Vitez, who also worked in the same company, Masino Gradina, which is where I worked. I also recognised the son of Jozo Matkovic from the village of Rijeka. I also recognised the brother of Dragan Matkovic, who used to go to school with me and Jako Krizanac from Krizancevo village. I recognised other people too, I knew them by sight, so these were people from Vitez or the places around Vitez. After this group --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, can I interrupt you at this point? Can we just confirm that the arrow on the photograph marked 5 shows the movement of these 30 or 40 soldiers that you saw coming from Zume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the direction from which they came and this is how they were spread out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many military policemen were amongst them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were five to six military policemen. The rest were wearing military uniforms and as I said, there were six to seven men with weapons, but they were wearing civilian clothes. I think that Blaz Totic was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any badges on these soldiers that would indicate to which army they belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I noticed on a soldier who was closest to me, it was the special unit with the chequerboard. I did not pay too much attention to these insignia, but in any event, I saw that Ivica Safradin was leading this group. He was the first to arrive there and then he was pointing them to the positions that they were to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you saw the chequerboard, the red and white chequerboard flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which means that these were Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think now is an appropriate time to finish, if you wish. We can carry on this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until 2.30 pm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume our hearing. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, that is Mr. Abdulah Ahmic, I would like to point out that because of the ceremonies next Monday, when our new colleagues will take their oath, we will stop from 4.00 to 5.00 this afternoon. We will have a one hour break and we will start then again at 5.00 and go until 6.00, unless the interpreters have reached the end of their tether and cannot go on. At that point, we will see whether they have the stamina to go on. We will not ask them to take the role of the judges. I do see both counsel standing, which is a wonderful and special favour for the Tribunal, since I think we will ask Mr. Hayman who wanted to say something, or perhaps Mr. Cayley. Mr. Hayman, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, may I? I apologise for interrupting and I do not want to take significant time from the court but there is a matter the Defence feels it needs to put on the record. If the usher could assist by placing a document on the ELMO and distributing it. This pertains, your Honour, to the redirect examination yesterday of Colonel Watters. He was examined concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I was not sure what you were talking about. Okay, you are talking about Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Bryan Watters. I am not seeking any relief at this time, I am not seeking a response or explanation from the Prosecution, we intend to file a written brief on this incident, but I wanted to raise it at the first opportunity, because we do believe it is very important. The court may recall, during the redirect examination, there was testimony concerning the offer of a cease-fire by Colonel Blaskic on 18th April 1993, and that was an offer which Colonel Watters characterised as a naive and blatant attempt to grab land. It was an offer that was never agreed to by the Army of BiH, according to Colonel Watters. We have obtained, since the conclusion of that -- if this could be put on the ELMO, please, so there can be a sight translation -- we have obtained a portion of the Mil Info Summ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am wondering about something. I know -- I am intentionally interrupting you before we get into the wrong track. I see that Mr. Kehoe is standing now. Am I to understand that you want to raise the issue of a reply to a reply? Ordinarily, only the Prosecution replies to your cross-examination, if I have understood that correctly. Before we go any further, let us be very clear about this. You are indicating a document which in some ways could be, from the point of view of method, interpreted a right to reply to the reply, which will be something new and it will be the first time this has happened. Before we even look at the document, could you first give us a few short words of explanation as to the principle, as this is the first time this is occurring and that is to have the examination, cross-examination, then the right to reply and then a reply to the reply, I am not even sure what to call it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Re-cross is the term, your Honour. We do not know what the proper remedy is. What I seek to put on the record today, so it is clear when we learned this and what our position is, is a very serious violation of the Prosecutor's obligations under Rule 68, namely that while they were eliciting testimony from Colonel Watters -- Rule 68 provides that exculpatory information and information that may tend to affect the credibility of a Prosecution witness must be disclosed to the Defence. While they were eliciting testimony from Colonel Watters that then Colonel Blaskic was engaged in a naive land grab and had not in good faith agreed to a cease-fire, that there had been no cease-fire, so that Colonel Blaskic's later complaints of a violation of the cease-fire were, I think, absurd and ridiculous, which was how Colonel Watters phrased it, while they were eliciting that testimony, they had in their possession a portion of the Mil Info Summ from April 18th 1993, which had been redacted from the version that was provided to the Defence, which clearly provides, and I quote from the first full paragraph, last sentence, it may be highlighted on some of your copies: "Commanding officer 1 Cheshire has agreed with 3rd Corps BiH and Central Bosnia HVO that the national cease-fire signed by Boban and Izetbegovic should be effective from 23.59 B hours tonight." I can represent to the court, this is a page that was redacted from the Mil Info Summ of 18th April 1993 that was given to us, we have obtained it from our own confidential sources, and thank goodness we were able to get it, because we should have had it a long time ago, it was exculpatory, and we certainly should have had it, as after Colonel Watters testified to the absolutely opposite proposition, that there was no cease-fire and he blamed Colonel Blaskic for acting inappropriately with respect to that subject. I simply wanted to put that on the record. We will file a legal brief on this by Monday or Tuesday, I am not sure what the remedy is, but I felt we had an obligation to raise it and bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I am not blaming you for having asked for the floor when there are serious issues involved, whether they come from the Defence or the Prosecution. It is absolutely legitimate to raise the issue. We must have living discussions and nothing should be fixed once and for all. I am sorry that in the procedure that we must carry through, the discussions are sometimes too closed off one from the other, you know, that is part of my system for which I am not blaming you. Secondly, I am asking that you file the brief as you said you would, with the proof, the evidence that you can bring to support what you are saying, but it is also correct that I ask Mr. Kehoe to supply some explanations, even if they are only partial and even if Mr. Kehoe or Mr. Harmon respond to your brief in writing. I would turn now to Mr. Kehoe to respond to the serious accusations which have been stated by Mr. Hayman. As you see in Rule 68, it says: "The Prosecutor shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the Defence the existence of evidence known to the Prosecutor which in any way tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or may affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence." We are all conscious here of the fact that we are all professionals. A document can be ambiguous and sometimes the Prosecutor is not able to know in advance whether the document will be exculpatory. There are documents which are obviously exculpatory, but there are others which are more subtly exculpatory. However, the point raised here is somewhat different, it would appear that in the document which you provided to the Defence, you in some way failed to give the entire document to the Defence. We are not accusing you here of anything, you will have the opportunity to respond in writing if necessary, but since the question has been raised, interrupting the rest of the proceedings and in an impromptu manner, I wonder whether you have any explanations which you could give us immediately before these things are put into writing in briefs which both you and the Defence will file. Mr. Kehoe, would you prefer to reflect about what I have just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can fill in the facts that counsel left out when he was discussing this right now, and that has to do with what the Prosecution actually did give to the Defence. If we look to the bottom of the particular page that counsel is referring to, there is an annex to that, that is the cease-fire agreement itself, the one that was introduced into evidence by Defence counsel. In the spirit of exculpatory evidence, that is what the Office of the Prosecutor gave to the Defence. That particular issue, the 18th April cease-fire signed by Blaskic, was not the subject of direct examination. This particular issue came up in cross-examination. Counsel asked Colonel Watters what he thought of this particular cease-fire agreement which he, in his opinion, gave short shrift to, because it had not been negotiated, neither by ECMM or by BritBat. At the time we were having this discussion, I candidly was not aware of one sentence in literally thousands of pages of Mil Info Summs, Mr. President and your Honours. Nevertheless the particular cease-fire agreement was given to the Defence as part of discovery and was brought out during cross-examination, not on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that this is a relatively complex question. I therefore think that for the time being we will resume our work today and I invite Mr. Hayman and Mr. Harmon or Mr. Kehoe, first Mr. Hayman, to file a brief to the Tribunal and in the brief, the charges will be indicated and the response can be filed by the Prosecution. I would also like to point out that if I recall correctly, it seems to me that Colonel Watters did not attach very much importance to that cease-fire since according to him, he had not -- it had not been -- the signature of that document had not been authorised by the other party, at least that is what it appeared. Mr. Hayman is therefore invited to present a brief to the Tribunal. If despite the Prosecutor's explanations he continues to request such a brief, if Mr. Kehoe feels that he has additional explanations to give, he can also respond in writing and that point will be settled later. Thank you. Usher, could we please have the witness brought in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on that point, the Prosecutor will gladly bring Colonel Watters back for further examination, if the court desires it. We can take that up any time the court wants to do that. That is certainly open for any opportunity and we will bring Colonel Watters back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That would be a possible solution, but the Tribunal will decide on that issue once we have read what you will have written. For the time being, we have not reached that point, and we are asking that Mr. Abdulah Ahmic be brought in. (Pause). The Registrar has just mentioned that he needs to know how the exhibit is going to be put in. For the time being, it relates to an incident which has been raised by the Defence who will produce the document. This document in my opinion will be attached once again in the annex in the application which Mr. Hayman will present. It will be the subject of the Prosecutor's answers. Only at that point and according to the solution which will be arrived at for that incident we will see whether or not it should be attached as a document in the file. It seems premature for that. For the time being, the transcript indicates that he will be able to put that into the record for the time being, but only once it has been indicated that it interrupted the proceedings here. We can now have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Abdulah Ahmic, please be seated. Do you hear me? Am I speaking loud enough? Do you hear me? Are you rested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you. Yes, I have rested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, your Honours, counsel. Good afternoon, Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Before the break, you were describing to the court the 30 or 40 soldiers that you had seen coming from Zume, and you had stated that the three-pronged arrow marked 5 on the aerial photograph represented those particular soldiers, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any other soldiers in the same area that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after this group that I saw, very shortly after them, another group of soldiers appeared --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, could you pause for a minute because the computer monitor is not showing the aerial photograph. There we are. If the usher could move it so it is straight? I am sorry for these interruptions, Mr. Ahmic. If you could please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I also apologise for interrupting, but in order to make things more concisely packed, since everybody has the drawing before him, perhaps it would be simpler for Mr. Ahmic to explain things, there is a photograph, there are numbers, maybe that would simply be easier, if that does not throw the pace of your questioning out of balance. That might be a solution. This may allow the witness a better opportunity to express himself spontaneously, if you think that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Ahmic. If within the course of your explanation you could refer to the aerial photograph as the President is suggesting, then I will not have to interrupt you to ask you to indicate what you are talking about in visual terms. So if you continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. After this group that I have already described who positioned themselves close to me, near group came, the size of a platoon, 30 to 40 soldiers, and they were going along route 6, and they also spread out. These soldiers, all of them, were wearing black uniforms. They are uniforms of the Ustasha army from the Second World War, as far as I know. Therefore they were the size of a platoon, that is 30 to 40 soldiers. They positioned themselves next to this group in this direction. As one of these soldiers was very close to me, here at point 4, I moved further down so that they would not see me in this hollow. When I reached this lower part, I saw that these houses down here were already on fire, my house, this house, this house (indicates), all these were already burning. So I stayed there and I saw these soldiers running around, but I did not pay much attention, so I was on this side of the road and watching more in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, when you moved across to the other side of the road to where the arrow marked 7 is, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw groups of soldiers coming from the direction at number 7 in my direction, and moving along the direction of the arrow to the right. During the day, I saw five or six such groups. They were very well equipped soldiers with weapons of great destructive might, RPGs, rocket launchers. Almost all of them had helmets, bullet-proof jackets. They were excellently equipped, and these groups consisted of ten to eleven soldiers each. All of them had different ribbons on their right hand shoulders. One group had red ribbons, another group white, another yellow, another green. In any event during that day five to six groups passed in this direction. They reached close to me and then they turned right as the arrow indicates. Shortly after that, I heard that nearby, a mortar had been brought in. I could hear it firing, it was probably hitting Ahmici, and an anti-aircraft gun was also brought there. I heard it, I did not see it. Then I could also hear some tanks, UN tanks passing by, and I heard some voices, but I could not understand because of the hum of the river and I was down there in the creek.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, did you identify any badges on the soldiers that you saw moving in the direction of the arrow marked 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some of them HVO insignia, some had HV insignia, yes, they did have insignia badges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, first of all with Exhibit 100/2, which is already in evidence, Mr. President. Is that one of the badges that you saw that day on the soldiers that were moving in the direction of the arrow marked 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is the emblem of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 116/2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the emblem of the HV, the Croatian army. There were some of these too and I devoted particular attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did you devote particular attention to that badge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my view, that was indication that the Croatian army was there too, because judging by how well equipped they were, they probably came from a different country and they had infiltrated themselves here, and these soldiers had these HV badges on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If the aerial photographs could be replaced on to the ELMO, please? Mr. Ahmic, you had been shot in the head earlier that day. How was your wound at this time? How did you feel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bleeding stopped quite quickly, so that I was not having any very great problems at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After seeing these groups of soldiers, what did you try to do next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there in that water the whole day and in the evening about 10.00 or 11.00, I decided to pull out, because I was all wet all day, so I headed in this direction (indicates) to this point 8. I had covered only five or six metres when I saw a dugout here which had been made earlier on, and I saw the little window, which surprised me, which meant that this had been prepared long ago to somehow secure this pass. So I covered five or six metres and saw at this point 8 three to four soldiers sitting on a fence and smoking. I could not pass by them, so I turned back to the other side of the road again, and then I moved along this route 7, and then I got to about 20 metres forward, but these houses were burning, this one, house number 3 and the stable next to it, then this house and stable, these two were burning, they are not marked (indicates), so it was light as if it was daytime so that they would not see me, I went back to point number 4. I took a rest and then going back, I saw at point 9 another three or four soldiers sitting and smoking on the other side of the road. I do not know whether they noticed me, I rested for about half an hour, and then I went in the opposite direction, this way, and I crawled along the stream past these soldiers and reached the position of Mujo Ahmic's house, position number 10. As soon as I had entered this house, I was noticed. The house was surrounded by two soldiers each from all four sides, they held me there all night. They did not do anything. I was surrounded. I dried up, the house was still smouldering, but there was some flame left, so I dried up and during the night, I noticed here (indicates) two men in white uniforms, I think they were European monitors. They were walking up and down, I saw them three or four times. I considered that strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you there, Mr. Ahmic? You said you saw two men in white uniforms to the right of the burnt house marked 10, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there in that house overnight. In the morning, six of them left, two of them stayed behind, one on each side and they were observing the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, just to return to the night, to that evening, did you see or hear anything that night in the vicinity of the house where you were lying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just saw these soldiers in white, nothing else of significance. I was not really interested because of what I had been through. I saw that I was surrounded again, so I did not know what I could expect, so I did not look around much that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I fell asleep for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, about 7.30 or 8.00, I heard the voice of my mother. She was here in Pero Papic's house at point 11, she had spent the night there and I heard her voice calling out, "what shall I do? They have killed my husband, my sons", she was wailing. I heard her but I could not see her because there was a fog, but I will tell you later how I learnt that she had spent the night there. So about 8.00, I heard that, and nothing else of significance until about noon. About noon, I noticed a vehicle coming from the direction of Busovaca to point 12, they stopped there, two military policemen came out and they headed in the direction of the village of Ahmici. The vehicle stayed behind. Shortly after that, somewhere around here, I noticed some black smoke, very thick black smoke, and shortly after that, I heard a very powerful explosion, it was probably the minaret of the mosque that was blown up then. A little later in the upper part of Ahmici village, that would be about 1.00, again explosions could be heard, rifle shots and several houses were set on fire, so that is that moment. Then these soldiers came back very quickly, they climbed into the vehicle and they came to where I was, point number 10. I saw that they had military police badges, I heard them talking, and this one who was guarding me said, "what is new in Busovaca?", and they answered, "nothing, everything is under control. What is new here?". He said, "I am holding a captured Mujahedin here, what are we going to do with him?". The other one said, "throw a hand grenade at him and kill him". I was sitting in the room here (indicates) and I saw his face well, he was fair, he had a cap, he had wavy blond hair, he was about 24 years old, 24 or 26. He threw a hand grenade, a black one, it fell about a metre from me. I watched it, I did not even move far away. It went off, all the walls were shattered by the fragments, it exploded right next to me, and the burnt remains of the house blew up into a cloud of smoke. It hit my head a little and my ear went deaf. I still cannot hear too well from that explosion on this area. Then these men who had come from Busovaca started to demolish -- there was a small factory, a small plant here under construction. This is it (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are indicating the building beneath the building that is ringed 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who did that factory belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cazim Ahmic, with a Croat from Vitez, had planned to open this factory, it was supposed to be producing washing powders and antifreeze liquid, so they demolished this factory, they set fire to a stable which had been burnt earlier and repaired; then they burnt it again. They also tried to set fire to a yellow Yugo, a Fiat. While they were doing this, I was sitting in the middle of the room coming to, so to speak, recovering, and then the one who had thrown in the grenade came in and another young boy, a 13 or 14 year old boy, he had a rifle and he had a camouflage cap and they were watching me. I again pretended to be dead. There were flames around me, I could have burnt so I had to turn over so as not to burn. They saw that I was alive and I think they watched me for an hour or two, maybe even three, they saw that I was alive. Finally, the little one said, "let us throw a couple of grenades at him. What are we waiting for to kill him". The older one said, "no, look there is some dynamite here, that will be more effective". So they jumped out of the window, I got up, I started calling them then, "boys, I am not a soldier, I am a civilian", but this probably surprised them, so they did not do anything. Then I saw Ivo Papic and Simo Vidovic, that is not marked, but they were here (indicates). I spotted them, I just waved to them and they came up to me into this room, or rather near the house, they asked, "who are you? What are you", and I said "save me, they are mistreating me here". "Come with us", they said and they took me out. Then we went in this direction --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you can stop there. That is fine. If you could just confirm for me on the aerial photograph that 1 -- what is the area marked 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the area marked 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Fahrudin Ahmic's house, my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the area marked 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 3, that is Hajra Ahmic's, she was my aunt, her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You referred earlier to hearing a large explosion from the area of the mosque. Can you point on the photograph again to the area where you think that explosion came from after the arrival of the two military policemen from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is it, here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you are pointing to the area and it says above it "Ahmici mosque minaret".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After the arrival of Papic Ivo and Simo Vidovic, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me to Zume, the settlement called Zume. On the way, Ivo told me, he said, "I took your mother and sisters to your lines in the direction of Vrhovine village and they took two cows with them". I said, "well, thank you", and I asked him if he could bury my father and brother and he said, "no, I will not be doing that, but there is somebody who is in charge of burying the dead". Then he took me to the Zume settlement: if I could please be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Another photograph, but first of all, what actually happened to your mother and sisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivo told me that he had escorted them to our lines, but somewhere towards the village of Ahmici, they probably came to upper Ahmici. They were probably killed by the explosions that I heard at about 1.00 pm and the shooting. The British officer Stewart, he confirmed that a woman with daughters was killed in a house and that was most probably when they were killed in that settlement there. In that interview of his, he was showing the house, pointing at the house and saying, "in this house, in front of the house, there were two dead men, a father and son were killed, they were trying to protect the mother and daughters who were down in the cellar. A maniac came, a HVO soldier, he threw a hand grenade into the basement, he used automatic fire against them and then he set fire to all of that". That is I think how they met their death in the upper Ahmici village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In any event, whether that account is correct or not, you have never seen your mother or three sisters again after 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If there are no objections from the Defence, Mr. President, I would like to move into evidence Exhibit 115, which is the aerial photograph that is on the ELMO at the moment, and if I could ask the usher to replace that aerial photograph with Exhibit 117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence? That is in fact 115, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you were explaining how Anto Papic told you that the burial of the dead was already organised and that it was not necessary for you to have to pay him any money to bury your father and your brother, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivo Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Ivo Papic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said to Ivo, "I have 400 Marks in my pocket, take it". He said, "no, I do not need money", but later I learned someone called Igor Calic, Miso's son, he unearthed my father and took the 400 Marks from him, so I learnt about this, that there were such cases too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said that the money was in your pocket; the money was in your father's pocket, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This next photograph depicts the lower portion of the road coming down from Ahmici towards Santici. Am I right in saying that on this particular day, on the 17th April you were escorted down this road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was 17th April, yes. Yes, that is correct, I was going along this road, it was Saturday 17th April --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, while you were proceeding down the road, did you observe on either side of the road the houses of the Muslim residents of Ahmici and the commune of Zume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less all the houses had been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you follow the numbers from 1 to 24 on this aerial photograph which you identified to me while we were speaking before your testimony, and can you tell the court what the state of the house was, and to the best of your knowledge what happened to the occupants of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I will tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you start with 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a bit too far away for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can do what we did a little while back so that the witness can speak as spontaneously as possible. He has the map in front of him, I think everyone else has the picture. Could he not simply take each of the numbered houses, say what Muslim family was the owner of that house, what happened to the owners? I think that would be better for him. He would be less -- it would be easier for him than if he tried to use the pointer and to try to point out the numbers, because everybody has the same photo, including the Defence counsel. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 1 is the house of Hasim Ahmic, and his son Fahrudin, they were killed. Number 2, is the house of Ahmic Ezedin and his mother. Number 3 is the house of Mustafa Puscul, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, what happened to the occupants of the house in circle 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 2, he was not there, Ezedin at that moment was not at home. Only his mother was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to interrupt for a second. Since this is a public hearing, I would like to have the photo on the ELMO so the public gallery can see it as well, but this does not change anything about the method we wish to use. Mr. Ahmic, do not worry about the projector, it is for the public gallery to know what you are saying. Do it as spontaneously as you can, say what comes to your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, I was saying, house number 2, Ezedin Ahmic, he was not at home then, his mother was there. House number 3, Mustafa Puscul, he was killed. House number 4, Rasim Ahmic, the son of Ramiz, he was also killed. House number 5, Nazif Ahmic, and both Nazif and his son, who was a minor, were killed. House number 6, Ramiz Ahmic, he was killed as well as his son Ramsim. House number 7, Islam Ahmic, he was killed. Then here is number 8, Sefik Ahmic's house, he was killed too. House number 9, Nesib Ahmic's house, his son Elvedin was killed, but he was not at home at the time, he was away, he was in Croatia, so he was captured and held in a camp in Mostar. He is now alive. Houses 12, 13 -- 11, 12 and 13, I do not know exactly the owners, I cannot remember, but Adem Siljak was killed there and another two or three people were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, house number 10, was that a Muslim house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Number 10, 11, 12 and 13, I do not know exactly who the owners were, because I did not live there, but I know that three or four men were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: House number 14?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 14, this was the house of a man from Zenica, he came and settled there. He too was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: House number 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: House number 16, Ismail Ahmic, Ismail and his son Mujo were killed. House number 19 is Mehmed Ahmic's -- house number 17, I am sorry. That belonged to Mehmed Ahmic, he is alive. He was in a camp with me, he was not killed. He was wounded before the war in the head in a traffic accident. He was hurt in a traffic accident. House number 19 is Sabiha Djidic's, or rather house number 18. Her two sons were killed, Muharem and Nedzad. House number 19 is Nedzad's house. House number 20 is Mustafa Pezer's house, we called him Ibrahim. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted) and Sakib Pezer's house, Pezer was killed and his son Mevludin. Sakib and his son Mevludin. House number 24 was Meho Hrnjic's. Both Meho and his son were killed. I do not recall the name of his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, what was the state of all of these houses as you walked down the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all burnt down, there was not a single one still burning when I passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there houses that were intact by the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the Croatian houses were absolutely intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed you can see that from the aerial photograph that many of the houses still have their roofs on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are those houses, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If there is no objection from the Defence, I would like to apply for Exhibit 117 to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, this is 117?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, this is Exhibit 117.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 118. Mr. Ahmic, before we get to this photograph, which location were you taken to by these two individuals after you left the settlement of Zume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to a house, I think it is the third, the photograph is from a great distance here. I think it was the third house going in that direction. I cannot see Santici in this photograph -- in fact Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do not be concerned with this photograph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the third house from the road in Zume in the direction of Pirici looking on the right-hand side, third or fourth house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you got to this house, what did you find at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the house when they brought me there, Ivo and Simo, there was Ivo's uncle Anto, he was carrying a M 48 rifle and he was guarding the house. I found in my estimate about 100 people there, Muslim women and children and about three or four elderly men who had not been killed. So that was some kind of a collection point. I was also brought in there and I spent the whole night there. In the morning, around 8.00, Nikica Plavcic came, he was a painter in Vitez. "I have good news for you, I am taking you to be exchanged in Dubravica, in the school in Dubravica", so we started in this direction, it was a long file of people, maybe up to 500 metres long. We were going down the road, there is the UNPROFOR base here (indicates). I do not know how it came that nobody from there ever helped us. So he took us there by himself to this school in Dubravica, which is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What do the two marks on the photograph indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the length of the group of the people that was walking along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the camera could be brought out now, could you please point on the photograph to the location to which you were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the school in Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is here, the school building (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the purposes of the record, the witness is pointing to the building with the label marked "Dubravica school". Mr. Ahmic, can you describe the scene that you saw when you entered the Dubravica school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered into the school yard, I was the last one in the group. The moment we all came in, again these were special units, they had insignia on their shoulders, closed the door behind us. We immediately understood that this was not an exchange, that this was a camp. They started separating out younger women to the right and the rest were put in the gym. I was shown to go to the left to the gym, and there we found 30 to 40 adult men who had been brought from the suburbs of Vitez, from Rijeka, from Novaci, Gacice and other places. They had been brought there just prior to us, a couple of hours before we did. We were all in this gym, in this building. The same night, new groups of arrested -- mostly these arrested civilians started arriving, some adult men. During the night they started taking groups of ten people to dig trenches and they were taking them to the frontlines in Santici, Krcevine, Nadioci and all around Vitez, I do not know the locations. So they started taking people out to dig trenches. This went on throughout the time I was there. Some people would come back wounded and one person even died. We were told that he died from a sniper bullet. I think his name was Tuso. He was from Nadioci. He was digging trenches and was shot by a sniper. I stayed in the camp five to six days. I did not have any medical care and the food was bad. The last day of my stay in the camp, I noticed that some women were raped. A wife of a man who was lying next to me came over and she was crying and I understood what had happened based on the conversations that they had. I understood that the women who had been separated out to the right had been taken and there were incidents of them being raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why were you not taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was more severely injured, I was not taken. There was Anto from Krizancevo village with a moustache, he was the commander in the camp. His deputy head with a blue arm band, similar to the blue arm bands that those two who were shooting us, they also had that, I forgot to say that. I do not know what his name was, but he also had that blue arm band. Then it was not him, somebody else came, I do not know where he was from, but he was quite strict and so he pointed me, "you", and I got up and I said, "I am wounded, I cannot", and he said, "get up", so I started and Anto said, "no, let him go, he is wounded", so I was not taken out to dig. Had I been taken, I do not know, I think I would have fainted. I could not -- I was too weak and I was all swollen. Then a CBS TV team came, that was the next to last day there, I do not know if they are Canadian or American television, and then also the Red Cross came and registered us and gave us these ID cards that they give out. Then the following day a medical team arrived. There were five of us who were considered serious medical cases and we were taken to the hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That was on 23rd April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, that is about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said that there was a special unit that was running the Dubravica school. I would like to show you a badge now to see if you recognise it, and if the usher could assist, this is Exhibit 116/3. If you could wait one moment, Mr. Ahmic? Is that the badge that you saw worn on the arm of the soldiers who were at the Dubravica school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, probably. I can read, I could read this. "Postrojba Posebne Namjene", which means "Special Purpose Unit". At one point, the so-called HOS people were there, there was the Croatian -- at some point they had been disbanded after a conflict with the HVO, but they were under the command of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it was your impression that this unit was under HVO command at this time in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively. Because one day in the camp, they read us some letter from their supreme command, so that meant that they had a command, their top command in Vitez. This was about the establishment of the Croatian state, so that was read to us, this proclamation. This was made official to us, so that means that they were under the command of the HVO, this unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So on 23rd April, you were taken to Zenica where you were treated for your wounds, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I would like to show you a number of photographs, not too many, in fact only six, which you have provided to me and which -- some of which you have identified to me, others of which you provided to me. First of all, if the witness could be shown Exhibit 47? Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the masjid, this is a religious structure in the central part of the Ahmici village called Grabovi and it is destroyed, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who built it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was built by the contributions from the inhabitants of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you involved in the construction of this building yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 116/4. Mr. Ahmic, do you recognise this photograph which I in fact showed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the burnt house of my -- Sakib Ahmic, my uncle. This is the kitchen, this is the stable and then in the back was his house (indicates). This is right next to the highway, Travnik/Zenica and Busovaca/Vitez, that is where the house is. This is the road to Ahmici, this here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown Exhibit 116/5. This is a photograph that I showed to you, Mr. Ahmic, and you identified it for me. What is this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the destroyed house of Sakib Ahmic, my uncle. That is the same house that I referred to before, which is next to the road Zenica/Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown photograph 116/6? Where was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph was taken in the summer kitchen at the structure I saw, of Suljeman Ahmic, son of Sakib, and this is a birthday celebration. This is my uncle, Sakib, who was killed in the house which I showed before, his wife Sadeta, and this is Suljeman. You can see all of him. This was his summer kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So your uncle Sakib and his wife Sadeta were killed on 16th April, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were killed, and their son Semir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What year was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think two or three years before the HVO attack on our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 116/7? Where is this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a house in Grabovi and it belongs to Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There is not a mark on this house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is obvious. Here, this is the house of Sukrija Ahmic, you can see that it has been burnt down, it has been destroyed. It is clear whose house remained intact and who was attacking and who was destroying. Sukrija was killed. His brother Naser, which was a baby of two months, two months baby and his wife. It was all in the vicinity of Vlatko Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was Vlatko Kupreskic a Bosnian Muslim or a Bosnian Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is a Bosnian Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now the last two photographs, first of all photograph 116/8. Who is this a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a paragraph of my mother when she was still a young woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is this the only photograph that you have of Latifa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the last photograph, which is 116/9, if you could point out on that photograph to me, Mr. Ahmic, the two persons relevant to this proceeding that you identified to me earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Semir, son of Sakib Ahmic, my uncle. He was killed in the house which I showed previously. This is Alma, my youngest sister, she was also killed. At that time she was 16 when she was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So this photograph was taken a little time before the attack on Ahmici, but again this is the only photograph you have of your sister.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is not a few years, several years, maybe eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe five to six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After you fled from Ahmici, am I right in saying that you joined the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I joined the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were demobilised in 1996, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think now you are working in Zenica, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Ahmic, just to make matters absolutely clear to the court, am I right in saying that during the attack on Ahmici on 16th April 1993, you lost every single member of your family, apart from your brother Munir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the attack I lost my whole family, with the exception of my brother Munir. But unfortunately he was also killed after, during an HVO attack on the frontlines, so I am actually the only one remaining of the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. I would like to apply purely for housekeeping purposes for the admission of all of the exhibits, which I can number off if the Registrar wishes and certainly if the Defence have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is the entire photograph album. You have got the aerial photograph, that is 118, right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, there is Exhibit 118 which has to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence to 118 being admitted as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have no objection, except for a question for the Prosecutor about one of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are now dealing with the numbering of this photo album. Will the whole album be counted as one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the album is 116 and each of the photos has a different number, so it is 116/1, 2, 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see Mr. Hayman is showing us one of the photos. Perhaps he has an objection to make before they are filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The witness has identified this patch, your Honour, I think it may be 116/3, but on our copy there appears to be something at the top that has been drawn over or blacked it. There is some confusion over who created it, is this a picture of a patch or a drawing of a patch? If this is a photocopy that has been altered in some way, at least I want to make sure everybody's copy has been altered in the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, I can sustain that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can clarify the point very easily, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness was able to identify a badge in the format in which you see before you. There were certain words on the copy of the badge from our source which he could not identify for me, so the most accurate and true representation of what the witness said he saw and he described to me is in the format before you now. There is no trickery, no magic, it is a simple explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I guess what we would prefer and I will leave it to the court is if the Prosecutor knows that a particular badge actually exists, the witness can say, "this is what I saw but I cannot say I saw the letters" so we all know what were the letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is the kind of incident that we can avoid. I understand that the Defence asks this question. Mr. Cayley, you have to try to avoid this kind of thing, because then I have to ask the question of the witness who has just told us he has lost his whole family to tell us what is on this emblem. I am very sorry, I understand this tragedy of which you were the victim, Mr. Ahmic. We have great feeling for that, but for clarity of our legal discussions, can you remember what was on that emblem? Otherwise the Prosecution has to give us a given copy of it. Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, the patch as such, the important part is the chequerboard, because all Croatian units use this chequerboard, and to me the most important part is that I noticed this chequerboard and I cannot discuss the shape of the letters, but I did not invent the letters and what was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn to the Prosecution, Mr. Cayley, could you have a copy, I know this is not easy, there are too many exhibits in here which are not explained, but perhaps you could do something so that the exhibit can be put into the files or into the record, otherwise -- other than the way it is right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I just confer with my colleagues one moment? (Pause). Mr. President, we are perfectly happy to put the patch in as it was before. The reason that was done, and I emphasise this to the court and to Mr. Hayman, was to present an entirely truthful account of what the witness was able to say about this badge. I am perfectly happy to put the badge in its full format, but I object very strongly to any implied allegation that I have doctored evidence in some way, because that was not my intention at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There is no such accusation, your Honour. We are just concerned as to whether this is an actual patch or a drawing or a hybrid, or what, so that it is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Tribunal understands that no one is questioning Mr. Hayman's honesty here. All right, we will start again at 5.00 after suspending the hearing right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are now resuming our hearing. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The final matter, Mr. President, is the matter of the badge. I provided a copy of it to the Defence and to the court. If it could be placed in front of the witness and he will be able to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, would you please give us an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the emblem that I saw on two occasions, the first time when I was hidden, and I remember well that I read these words, "Postrojba Posebne Namejene", "Special Purpose Unit", and the chequerboard flag . As for "Vitezovi", I did not pay much attention to that, but I was intrigued by this name, "Special Purpose Unit", so I assume they must be some kind of special units. Also in the camp I devoted more attention to these words, the "special purpose unit". That is my explanation. As for the word "Vitezovi", I cannot claim 100 per cent that I saw that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. I think now the Defence is reassured and we can incorporate this document as an exhibit, if there is no objection from the Defence, and it will be assigned -- we will use the old number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think the best thing would be to number it as 116/3 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, on the basis that all the exhibits are now in evidence, I have no further questions for the witness on examination-in-chief and I can offer the witness for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As in all equitable and fair trials, the accused has two counsel, and one of them will ask you a certain number of questions and this is known as the cross-examination. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good evening, Mr. Ahmic. My name is Anto Nobilo, one of two members of the Defence counsel of General Blaskic. I am sorry to have to bother you, the Defence certainly commiserates with you for all that has happened, but I have to ask you a few questions. Talking about this emblem, were the relationships of the letters as it is? Was this the proportion of the letters between the words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot claim that with certainty, but I can claim that that is what was written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At the beginning, you said that in the area where you were living, there were Croats and Muslims and a few Serbs. Were there any Romanies in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were they a significant group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were a small group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, in 1992, did you perhaps have any joint guard duties with the Croats in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not. We did meet, but we did not have any joint guards, but the guards would meet, exchange a few words but then each one went on his own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You never had jointly organised guard duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a little of that in the woods, but not in the settlement in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why did you have those guards in 1992? Where did the danger threaten from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The danger threatened from torchings, lootings and unforeseen contingencies, from the possibility of the infiltration of sabotage groups, because a war was being waged not far away, so it is normal to have such guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where was the closest frontline, the frontline with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vlasik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many kilometres away is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think 200 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The special purpose factories, I think that is how we used to call them in our country, that is the military industry, who was the owner, do you know who owned them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were state-owned enterprises; however, the Croats had a decisive role in those enterprises. At first the Serbs, later the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that it was the Federal Secretariat of National Defence of former Yugoslavia, they were the owners of those factories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but after the conflict in Slovenia and Croatia, the Croats had the main say there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know who was the general manager, the technical manager?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, I know a technical manager, Santic, one of the indicted, Santic, who was President of the municipality in Vitez. He was the technical manager in Sintevit, I know him personally because I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But tell me, were there any Muslims in the management?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you were "put on hold". What exactly do you mean? What were your rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Waiting. The west does not understand that. I do not know how to put it. I cannot claim that there was no work, but people were systematically laid off so as not to have insight into what was happening in the military industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this did not mean losing one's job, but it was just being temporarily at home because there was no work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During the war, and all the circumstances in the former Yugoslavia, was there a reduction in the amount of work available? There was a collapse of the system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To some extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were the Croats laid off too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know what were the results of the first elections in Vitez municipality, roughly who won?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. The HDZ won in the local elections, but they had a small majority, but the SDA won in the BH Parliamentary elections in terms of the number of deputies. Sero Muharem won in the second round of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So HDZ, the Croatian party, won in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was a very close victory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, you told us that there was virtually a military government in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you give us a few examples to illustrate what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the military rule of the HVO is concerned, in 1992, I was told this in person by Mladen Marinic, when these people -- when we had the vote for the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina so I asked him how were things in the HDZ, and he said "the HDZ is not affected, we have the HVO rules", so I had first-hand information that the Croats had formed their own HVO authority, not the HDZ authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croats in Bosnia called both the army and the civilian authorities by the name of HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on the HVO became everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The civilian or the military HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In my view, it was a military administration more than a civilian one. It was not a civilian one. It was in fact in preparation for the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was the President of the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivan Santic, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he a military man or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was the Vice-President of the municipality, or the President of the executive board, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fuad Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he a civilian or a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a civilian, but -- may I? It was minimised, their work was minimised in my opinion, because I know Kaknjo would tell me the Croats would discuss who would be doing what, so that the Croats were already taking over all the leading, how shall I put it, results, they channeled everything into their -- for their own benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that after some time, there were actually two civilian authorities, a Muslim and a Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was -- the separation was gradual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a Municipal Assembly meeting or other meetings that were held in Vitez at the municipality level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was a member of the SDA, so I would learn about things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Finally for this part of my examination, do you believe that the Croats edged the Muslims out of authority, or was it the military wing of the Croats that excluded the Muslims from the organs of authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the military wing of the HVO took over all power among the Croats as well as over the entire municipality of Vitez. You know very well that the Muslims had to sign allegiance to Herceg-Bosna or they had to leave the municipality. I do not know whether you are aware of that. I could give you the names of two people, Mustafa Ahmic and a man from Kruscica who was a porter in the municipality, he had to sign this document of allegiance to hold on to his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A loyalty to the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the civilian, but the civilian was actually a military authority, a military government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Give us some specific examples from which you infer that it was the military wing that held authority in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, the words of Mladen Marinic, who said, "the HDZ is not functioning, it is the HVO that is functioning". Ask Mladen Marinic from Nadioci. He was President of the HDZ in Nadioci and already then they were distributing ammunition, people were voting for the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and people went up to Mladen saying, "give me a rifle, bombs, grenades", so the contingents were coming to the Croats from Croatia in 1992. Believe me, I witnessed this. There were people in military uniform coming to cast their votes. His name was Carlo, and Livancic -- let me think. The son of -- I cannot remember. That was already in 1992, two men in military uniform, that was the first time I saw them in uniform in 1992, so you must see that that was already then a military organisation, and that Mladen Marinic said to me, "it is the HVO that is in power, the HDZ is not operative".

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 1992, had not the war with the Serbs already started? Was it not normal for people to be in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there was a war in Croatia, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There was no war in Bosnia still in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It started in 1992, in April, when Mladen Marinic said to me, was talking to me, that was when the barricades started, but when Mladen Marinic was talking to me there was no war in Bosnia, this was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you have any other examples which show that the army had taken over power in the municipal bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, in schools the Croatian curriculum was introduced, our children were not willing to attend those courses, and the joint Croatian and Muslim authorities would never have agreed to such a measure, but it was the military that imposed such a programme to be introduced in the schools, so you see there was somebody above the civilian HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. The Croats imposed their curriculum in the schools, but how can you conclude from that that it was the military wing that had imposed this and not the civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because in my view, they had not made any arrangement with the Muslims. A compromise should have been found, so they did what they wanted, according to their own wish. The Croats are like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But how do you conclude from that that it was the military, the army that imposed this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they probably had a document to that effect. I have no evidence, but there must have been some kind of a regulation among you for this to be solved in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you never saw such a paper or a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you have any other evidence that the army took over power?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, objection. The question has been asked five times now about evidence. The witness is trying to explain as best as he can from his experience what he saw. Counsel should be asked to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I sustain the objection. He did not come here with documents or written papers to prove what he witnessed or what he did not witness. Please move on to another question, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I agree that it was sufficient and that is why I asked the question, to see what it was the witness actually saw and experienced. Mr. Ahmic, you said in the examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor that people from Herzegovina had come to protect the factory, the factory of explosives. When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was -- I think it was in 1993 and maybe even before that. You know that there was a conflict in Busovaca before the conflict in Vitez, and we know for sure some of our people were working in that factory and they told us that some people from Herzegovina had come and they were watching over the factory. This was the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did they leave the factory, if they left it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, perhaps that army is still there, your army. I do not know when they left it, but they were there until the HVO attack on Ahmici, I think they were there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of your examination-in-chief that the TO was actually civil defence among you. What did you want to say? What is "civil defence"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is this concept of civil defence, we had it in our educational system before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am sure you have read about it and studied it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me explain a little. It serves to protect property and lives, as we Bosnians could not, like the Croats, form an army because we were surrounded within zones, so we limited ourselves to civil defence. We had little weapons, we could not create any army. As far as Ahmici is concerned, the little weapons we had were of a poor quality, burnt, that had been brought over after the explosion in Slimena, and we hardly had any ammunition, so we cannot talk about any real army. We called it Territorial Defence, to try and protect ourselves, at least to some extent, from any enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Does civil defence, according to what we learnt at school in the former Yugoslavia, does it have weapons or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
